title: Land Cells Cut Off From the Edge
statement:
You get a grid of 0 (water) and 1 (land). From a land cell you may step up, down, left or right onto another land cell. Diagonal steps are not allowed.

A land cell escapes if some walk over land reaches a cell on the outer border of the grid (from there you can step off the map). Return how many land cells cannot escape.

examples.why: The 1 at the left edge escapes directly. The three connected cells in the middle are surrounded by water.
The bottom cell of the shape is inside, but the shape touches the top edge, so every cell in it can walk out.
The lone 1 at (1, 1) touches the next shape only diagonally, which does not connect. The other shape reaches the bottom edge, so only (1, 1) is stuck.

hints: Instead of asking for each cell whether it can escape, ask the reverse: which land cells can be reached from the border?
Start a flood fill from every land cell on the border and mark everything it reaches.
The answer is the number of land cells left unmarked. Use an explicit stack or queue: a 500 × 500 snake of land would overflow a recursive DFS.

explain.intuition:
Checking every land cell separately repeats the same search over and over. Flip the direction: walking is symmetric, so a cell can reach the border exactly when the border can reach the cell. Flood-fill from all border land cells at once and mark what you touch.

Everything marked can escape. Every land cell left unmarked is stuck, so count those. It is the same move as finding all DOM nodes that are still attached to the document by walking down from the root, instead of walking up from each node.
steps: Push every land cell in the first and last row and the first and last column onto a stack, and mark it (for example, set it to 0 in a copy).
Pop cells and push each unmarked land neighbor, marking it as you push.
When the stack is empty, count the land cells that were never marked.
pitfalls: Treating diagonal neighbors as connected. Only four directions count.
Recursive DFS on a 500 × 500 grid: a long winding island exceeds the call stack in both JS and Python.
Marking cells only when popped instead of when pushed, which pushes the same cell many times.

solutions.title: Search from every land cell
solutions.idea: For each land cell run a BFS and see whether it reaches the border.

solutions.title: Flood fill from the border
solutions.idea: Mark everything reachable from border land; what remains is stuck.

followups: Return the number of stuck islands instead of stuck cells.
Solve it with union-find, joining every border cell to a virtual 'outside' node. When is that version handy?
